title: Getting Around Bodrum: Dolmuşes, Ferries and the Airport
excerpt: Bodrum has no metro and no city bus network of its own: the peninsula runs on cooperative dolmuşes timetabled by Muğla's MUTTAŞ, paid with the MuğlaKart or a contactless bank card, from a garage in the town centre that is not the intercity otogar. Summer timetables run past midnight and collapse in winter, the airport bus is timed to domestic flights, and the Kos ferry is a real border crossing with passport rules that catch people out.
bodyHtml:
No card to buy first — the peninsula runs on minibuses

There is nothing on rails in Bodrum and no city bus fleet of its own. Public transport on the peninsula is the dolmuş: minibuses owned by driver cooperatives, licensed by Muğla Büyükşehir Belediyesi as ÖTTA (özel toplu taşıma araçları) and timetabled by MUTTAŞ, the metropolitan municipality's transit company. MUTTAŞ lists them as numbered lines — 2-34 Bodrum–Turgutreis, 2-41 Yalıkavak, 2-45 Gümüşlük, 2-47 Gündoğan, 2-46 Göltürkbükü, 2-52 Gümbet, 2-1A Bitez, 2-28 Ortakent–Yahşi, 2-20 Torba — but nobody on the street uses the numbers: you read the destination board in the windscreen, flag the minibus down anywhere on its route and say where you want off.

Everything radiates from the Bodrum Merkez Garaj, the old otogar on Cevat Şakir Caddesi in Çarşı, a short walk uphill from the harbour — MUTTAŞ still labels it 'Bodrum Şehir Merkezi Eski Otogar'. Turgutreis and Yalıkavak have their own minibus garages, and the cross-peninsula runs linking Turgutreis, Gümüşlük, Yalıkavak, Gündoğan and Türkbükü start there, not in Bodrum.

Paying: MuğlaKart, bank card, and the cash question

The fare system belongs to Muğla Büyükşehir, so the card is the MuğlaKart — the municipality's pages also call it the Muğla Kent Kart — with the MuğlaApp (newer versions say 'muğlakart+') for balances, NFC and QR top-ups and live vehicle tracking. It works province-wide, on MUTTAŞ buses and ÖTTA minibuses alike. Anonymous cards and top-ups come from 24-hour dolummatik machines at the Merkez Garaj, the Torba terminal, the Turgutreis minibus stop (Karabağlı Caddesi No:19), the Yalıkavak minibus garage (Şeyhülislam Ömer Lütfü Caddesi No:25/A) and in Ortakent, Gündoğan, Gümüşlük and Gölköy. Discounted cards go through the municipality's application points; the document list is written for Turkish residents, so ⚠ VERIFY with your residence permit before assuming one.

You do not need the card on day one. Muğla Büyükşehir ended cash boarding on its own vehicles and the ÖTTA minibuses on 26 March 2020; what remains is the MuğlaKart, contactless bank cards and Android NFC phones, and every MUTTAŞ line page says 'tüm araçlarımızda kredi kartı geçerlidir'. Peninsula drivers are widely reported to still take cash — treat that as a favour, not a rule, and ⚠ VERIFY on your route. The card gets the discounted tariff; a bank card pays full fare.

Hours: summer runs past midnight, winter doesn't

Each MUTTAŞ line page carries a 'Son Güncelleme' stamp that tells you which season the table belongs to. The Yalıkavak line, updated 1 September 2026, shows the last minibus leaving the Merkez Garaj at 02:00 and Yalıkavak at 01:20; the Turgutreis line, stamped 24 June 2026, last leaves Bodrum at 01:30 and Turgutreis at 00:30. First departures are between 06:15 and 07:05. Between the two, the answer is a taxi.

The winter timetable trap. Those small-hours departures are the high-season table. Once the season ends the cooperatives thin the timetables — fewer vehicles, earlier last runs, long gaps on the smaller lines — and the MUTTAŞ site shows only the table in force today, not the one for the date you are planning. A late dinner in Yalıkavak in November needs a plan for getting back. ⚠ VERIFY winter last departures once the line page's update stamp changes in autumn; we found no published winter table.

Two otogars, and which one you want

The intercity terminal moved out of town in June 2021, to the Torba junction on the Bodrum–Milas road (Torba Mahallesi, Rıza Anter Caddesi 3012 Sokak): a 24-hour building with 21 intercity and 45 minibus platforms, built and run by Muğla Büyükşehir. No intercity ticket offices remain at the old otogar. At opening, MUTTAŞ and ÖTTA vehicles shuttled to the centre every five minutes — the 2-20 Bodrum–Torba line — ⚠ VERIFY the frequency now. The 48-1 Menteşe–Bodrum buses and the Milas minibuses also use Torba.

The airport: a bus timed to domestic flights

Milas–Bodrum (BJV) is 37 km from Bodrum. The one you can rely on is MUTTAŞ line 48-24: it leaves the town centre two hours before each domestic departure, picks up at the Torba otogar and at Jet Migros in Güvercinlik, calls at the international terminal on the way out, and on the return meets every domestic arrival. Bank cards work on board; the call centre is 444 48 01. Havaş is still listed on the airport's pages (old otogar – Torba – Güvercinlik – airport), but havas.net no longer has a Bodrum page and its only 2026 notice for the area is that the Didim–airport run stopped on 7 August 2026 — ⚠ VERIFY on 0850 222 0 487 before planning around it. Taxis wait 24 hours at both terminals (airport taxi cooperative +90 252 523 00 24) on the same meter tariff as in town.

Ferries: Kos, Kalymnos and the Datça car ferry

Two companies sail out of Bodrum. Bodrum Feribot (Bodrum Ferryboat, founded 1990, five vessels; +90 252 316 08 82) runs Bodrum–Kos, Bodrum–Datça and, from Turgutreis, Kos, Kalymnos, Leros and Patmos. Bodrum Express Lines (Çarşı Mahallesi, Barış Meydanı No:24; +90 252 316 10 87) runs Kos and Leros. Greek sailings leave from Bodrum Kale Port beside the castle or the Bodrum Cruise Port, and from Turgutreis D-Marin; in early September the Bodrum Express timetable showed daily Kos sailings through 1 November 2026, after which crossings thin to a few days a week — ⚠ VERIFY winter days with the operator, neither site publishes a winter table. Bodrum Express wants you at the port an hour before departure, Bodrum Feribot 30 minutes; both issue QR e-tickets.

The Kos passport trap. Kos is a Schengen border, not a day out on a boat. You need a passport — a Turkish ID card is not enough — and it goes through Turkish exit and Greek entry control both ways. Turkish citizens can get the Greek 'visa express' on arrival at Kos or Kalymnos: seven days, sixty euros, on a scheme Athens extended on 1 April 2026 through April 2027, and it does not let you continue to the mainland. Everyone else needs visa-free status or a Schengen visa before boarding — Bodrum Express's conditions say 'ordinary passport holders must have a valid Schengen visa prior to embarkation'. Since 10 April 2026 the EU's Entry/Exit System fingerprints and photographs non-EU passport holders on first entry, so allow time on the Kos side; ETIAS is not live yet. A passport with a Northern Cyprus (KKTC) stamp will be refused by the carrier. Open returns are valid a year but must be confirmed the day before.

The Datça ferry is domestic — an ID card does — and it carries cars: from Bodrum Kale Port (signed 'Datça Feribot İskelesi') across the Gökova gulf to the pier Bodrum Feribot calls Kairos Marina, the Körmen landing on Datça's north coast about 10 km from town, with minibuses meeting the boats; ⚠ VERIFY the two names are the same pier before you drive there. About two hours. Muğla Büyükşehir's timetable page, updated 24 August 2026, shows four sailings each way a day in summer; in winter it drops to a handful of days a week, and bad-weather cancellations are refunded.

Taxis

Bodrum has roughly 750 taxis. The meter tariff is set for the whole province by Muğla Büyükşehir's UKOME, raised most recently in spring 2026, and the meter is mandatory; there is no separate airport tariff. No number written here would survive the season, so the honest word is: expect the meter, and check that it runs. Bodrum to Yalıkavak or Turgutreis is 20-plus km, so a 03:00 taxi costs real money and the last dolmuş is worth catching.

Scooters, mopeds and bikes

Martı's shared e-scooters came to Bodrum in summer 2020; whether they are out this season is ⚠ VERIFY in the app — Martı's current city list does not name Bodrum. Rented mopeds and 125cc scooters are everywhere; shops advertise 'licence-free' 50cc models, but Turkish law still wants a licence matched to the engine and a helmet, and rental insurance rarely covers you without them. For cycling, the Güney Ege portal publishes a signed Bodrum Bisiklet Yolu along the Leleg Yolu — a signposted road route, not a separated lane.

Walking the centre, driving in season

Bodrum town is a walking place: the bazaar between the castle and the Merkez Garaj — Kale Caddesi, Cumhuriyet Caddesi along the front and the lanes between — is closed to cars on summer evenings. ⚠ VERIFY the closure hours with Bodrum Belediyesi; its kapalı yollar page lists roadworks, not the seasonal bazaar rule. Driving in July and August means one coast road and a single junction into each village; the dolmuş is usually faster. If you do drive, Bodrum Belediye A.Ş. runs the town car parks — Cevat Şakir (Çarşı Mahallesi, Cevat Şakir Caddesi No:41/1), the covered Pazar Yeri Altı (Yokuşbaşı Mahallesi, Külcü Sokak No:22/1), Çarşı, Kültür Sitesi and one in Gümüşlük — and Muğla Büyükşehir publishes a towing and impound tariff, which is what happens if you park in the bazaar.
